findings.title: GET /api/locks is unauthenticated and bypasses web basic auth
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the Atlantis HTTP port can enumerate every active project lock without any credential: repository full names, repo-relative project paths, project names, workspaces, pull request numbers and URLs, and the VCS username holding each lock. That is an internal-infrastructure map (private repo names, Terraform directory layout, who is deploying what and when) handed to an anonymous caller. Atlantis is routinely exposed to the internet because it has to receive VCS webhooks, so this is remotely reachable in the normal deployment. It also leaks in deployments where the operator believes the API is switched off: unlike every other /api handler, ListLocks does not check that APISecret is configured, so it serves data even when --api-secret was never set.
findings.evidence: server/middleware.go:36-45 exempts every path under /api/ from the web UI basic auth (`strings.HasPrefix(r.URL.Path, "/api/")` sets allowed = true), on the assumption that API handlers enforce the X-Atlantis-Token secret themselves. Every other API handler does: Plan and Apply go through apiParseAndValidate (server/controllers/api_controller.go:1009-1018 -- empty-secret check plus subtle.ConstantTimeCompare of the X-Atlantis-Token header), and DriftStatus, DetectDrift, Remediate, GetRemediationResult and ListRemediationResults each begin with `if !middleware.RequireAuth(w, r) { return }` (implementation at server/controllers/api_response.go:212-228). ListLocks (server/controllers/api_controller.go:383-408) has no auth call and no APISecret check at all -- it goes straight from the handler entry to `locks, err := a.Locker.List()` and serializes every lock into the response. The route is registered unconditionally at server/server.go:1212. The unit test encodes the behaviour rather than catching it: TestAPIController_ListLocks (server/controllers/api_controller_test.go:1309-1327) builds `http.NewRequest("GET", "", nil)` with no X-Atlantis-Token header and asserts http.StatusOK.
findings.recommendation: Add the same gate the sibling handlers use at the top of ListLocks: `middleware := a.getAPIMiddleware(); if !middleware.RequireAuth(w, r) { return }`. RequireAuth already returns 503 when APISecret is empty and 401 on a wrong/missing token, which is the behaviour the other endpoints have. Add regression tests asserting 401 for a missing token and for a wrong token, and 503 when no API secret is configured. Separately, make the middleware fail closed: instead of blanket-exempting the /api/ prefix from basic auth, exempt an explicit list of paths known to authenticate themselves, so the next handler added under /api/ is not silently public if its author forgets the check.

findings.title: websocket.NewWriter hard-codes CheckOrigin to always-true, silently discarding the --websocket-check-origin setting
findings.impact: NewWriter computes the correct origin-check function from the operator's --websocket-check-origin setting and then overwrites it one line later with a function that accepts every Origin. Any code path built on NewWriter would accept cross-origin WebSocket upgrades to /jobs/{job-id}/ws regardless of configuration, letting a page on an attacker-controlled site open a socket to an Atlantis instance the victim's browser can reach and stream live Terraform plan/apply output (which routinely contains resource names, account identifiers and sometimes secret values echoed by providers). Today the constructor is unreachable from production code -- the Multiplexor builds its Writer inline with the configured function (server/controllers/websocket/mux.go:45-57) and server.go:1062-1067 only calls NewMultiplexor -- so this is a latent trap rather than a live bypass, which is why it is rated low. Note also that --websocket-check-origin defaults to false (cmd/server.go:688-691), so the shipped default already allows cross-origin upgrades; that is a documented default but it makes the dead-code override easy to overlook.
findings.recommendation: Delete the `upgrader.CheckOrigin = func(r *http.Request) bool { return true }` line so NewWriter honours its own parameter, or delete NewWriter entirely since nothing calls it. Add a test that NewWriter(log, true) rejects a mismatched Origin, mirroring the existing TestCheckOrigin-style cases in server/controllers/websocket/mux_test.go. Consider flipping --websocket-check-origin to default true in a future major release, since the job-output socket carries Terraform output.

findings.title: Web basic auth falls back to the published default credentials atlantis:atlantis with no startup warning
findings.impact: An operator who turns on --web-basic-auth to protect the web UI, but does not also set --web-username and --web-password, gets the hard-coded, documented pair atlantis / atlantis. Everything the UI exposes -- the lock index at /, lock detail at /lock, live job output at /jobs/{job-id}, lock deletion at DELETE /locks, and the global apply lock at /apply/lock and /apply/unlock -- is then reachable by anyone who tries the default credentials. Deleting a lock and toggling the global apply lock are state-changing, so this is not purely a disclosure issue. The failure mode is silent: the server logs nothing to indicate that authentication is effectively open, and the flag name reads as though it alone provides protection.
findings.evidence: cmd/server.go:206-208 defines DefaultWebUsername = "atlantis" and DefaultWebPassword = "atlantis"; setDefaults (cmd/server.go:1066-1071) applies them whenever the operator left the values empty, independent of whether --web-basic-auth is on. The values are then copied verbatim into the middleware at server/server.go:1181-1183 and compared in server/middleware.go:46-53. The securityWarnings function (cmd/server.go:1322-1338) warns about every missing webhook secret but says nothing about default web credentials, and validate() (cmd/server.go:1076 onward) does not reject them. The default password is also printed in the public docs (runatlantis.io/docs/server-configuration.md:1705-1708).
findings.recommendation: Refuse to start when --web-basic-auth is enabled and the username or password is still the built-in default (or is empty) -- an error in validate() is the safest option. At minimum, add a line to securityWarnings such as "web basic auth is enabled but is using the default credentials; anyone can log in". Removing the defaults entirely and requiring explicit values when the flag is set is cleaner than warning.

findings.title: Web basic auth credentials compared with non-constant-time ==
findings.impact: The username and password supplied on every UI request are compared with Go's `==` string operator, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. That leaks a timing signal proportional to the length of the correct prefix, which in principle allows an attacker with a low-noise network path to recover the configured password byte by byte instead of guessing it. Exploitability over a real network is poor (the surrounding request handling dominates the signal), which is why this is low rather than higher, but the codebase already treats every other shared secret as timing-sensitive, so this is an inconsistency worth closing.
findings.recommendation: Compare with crypto/subtle, evaluating both halves so the result does not depend on which one failed, e.g. `userOK := subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(user), []byte(l.WebUsername)) == 1; passOK := subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(pass), []byte(l.WebPassword)) == 1; if userOK && passOK {`. Hashing both sides with SHA-256 before the comparison additionally removes the length side channel.

findings.title: Exported test helper DisableSSLVerification lives in production code and mutates the global HTTP transport
findings.impact: common.DisableSSLVerification sets InsecureSkipVerify on http.DefaultTransport, the transport shared by the whole process. While it is in effect, every outbound HTTPS call made through the default transport -- VCS API calls, webhook deliveries, binary and policy downloads -- accepts any certificate, so an attacker positioned on the network could intercept VCS tokens or feed back forged API responses. It is currently called only from server/events/vcs/azuredevops/client_test.go, so there is no live exposure; the risk is that it is exported from a non-test file, compiled into the shipped binary, and one production call site (or a future test that runs in parallel with real traffic, since the mutation is process-global and not scoped to a client) turns it into a real man-in-the-middle exposure.
findings.recommendation: Move the helper into a _test.go file (or an internal testing-only package) so it cannot be linked into the server binary, and have the tests point their VCS client at a custom *http.Client with its own TLS config instead of mutating http.DefaultTransport, which is shared process-wide and makes the relaxation racy under `go test -parallel`.

findings.title: External team allowlist command is assembled by string concatenation and executed through sh -c
findings.impact: The authorization decision for whether a commenter may run plan/apply is delegated to an operator-configured external command, and that command line is built by joining strings and handed to `sh -c`. The joined values include the repository full name and the user's VCS team names. If any of those ever contains a shell metacharacter, the injected text runs with the privileges of the Atlantis process -- which holds VCS tokens and cloud credentials -- and, because the checker treats a non-zero exit or an unexpected last line as "deny", an injection that changes the command's output to `pass` also grants the command authorization it was meant to withhold. On GitHub the exposure is currently theoretical: GetTeamNamesForUser returns team slugs (server/events/vcs/github/client.go:1122), which GitHub restricts to a safe character set, and repository names must pass the repo allowlist and models.NewRepo validation. The GitLab path uses operator-configured group names. So this is a robustness/defense-in-depth issue at present rather than a demonstrable injection, and it is rated accordingly.
findings.evidence:
server/events/external_team_allowlist_checker.go:49-61 builds the command:

	cmdArr := append([]string{checker.Command}, checker.ExtraArgs...)
	...
	orgTeams[i] = fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", ctx.BaseRepo.Owner, team)
	teamStr := strings.Join(orgTeams, " ")
	return strings.Join(append(cmdArr, command, ctx.BaseRepo.FullName, teamStr), " ")

and lines 27 and 37 execute it: `checker.ExternalTeamAllowlistRunner.Run(ctx, "sh", "-c", cmd)`. There is no quoting or escaping of any interpolated element, and teams are joined on a bare space so a team name containing a space silently becomes two arguments.
findings.recommendation: Pass the command as an argument vector rather than shell source -- the project already has exactly the right primitive for this in models.NewArgvCommandRunner (server/core/runtime/models/shell_command_runner.go:80), whose comment states it exists for commands Atlantis builds itself. Split the operator's configured command with shlex once at config-parse time, then append the command name, repo full name and each team as separate argv elements. If a shell must stay for backwards compatibility, validate every interpolated value against a strict allowlist (e.g. [A-Za-z0-9._/-]) and reject anything else rather than escaping it.
